Install these explicitly with patera[aiinterface], patera[desktop] or patera[desktop-ui] and the relevant provider extras. Keeping the bundle's scope avoids surprising existing server installations with desktop or machine-learning dependencies.

The production server is an extra too, prod, because a deployment needs it but a desktop program does not (it embeds Uvicorn). Without it, the core's dependencies are pure Python apart from pydantic-core.

items.title: Packages and imports
items.text: Every extension is a separate distribution that installs into the patera namespace. Distribution names use kebab case (patera-taskmanager); imports live under patera (patera.taskmanager). The full map is in the public API reference.

items.title: Next step
items.text: Continue with the quick start.

items.title: Project layout and auto-discovery
items.text:
When the application is created, Patera imports modules from well-known folders inside the application package and registers the classes it finds. A module is imported if its folder and file name match:

Kind Folders File name contains Registered when Controllers api, public, controllers, routers, routes api, controller, public, router, routes decorated with @path Exception handlers exceptions, exc_controllers handler, exception_controller, controller decorated with @exception_handler Middleware middleware, middlewares middleware, mw decorated with @middleware CLI controllers cli, cli_controllers, clis cli, cli_controller decorated with @cli_controller (CLI mode only) Loggers logging, loggers logger, log_sink, logging decorated with @logger

Folders are searched recursively. Include __init__.py files so the folders are packages.

A typical project:

app/
  __init__.py                              # @app class App(Patera[Config])
  configs.py
  api/
    __init__.py
    greeting_api.py                        # controllers
  controllers/
    page_controller.py
  middleware/
    request_id_middleware.py               # middleware
  exceptions/
    app_exception_handler.py               # exception handlers
  cli/
    tools_cli.py                           # CLI controllers
  logging/
    audit_logger.py                        # additional log sinks
  services/                                # not discovered: import what you use
  templates/
  static/

Models and services are not discovered

Only the component kinds above are discovered. Services, database models and other modules are used through imports and dependency injection.

items.title: Controlling discovery
items.text:
• Add folders with the CONTROLLER_FOLDERS, CLI_CONTROLLER_FOLDERS, EXCEPTION_HANDLER_FOLDERS, MIDDLEWARE_FOLDERS and LOGGER_FOLDERS options.
  • Classes marked with @ignore are skipped.
  • Classes (and endpoint methods) marked with @development are only registered when DEBUG is on.
  • Anything can also be registered explicitly with the register_* methods of the application: register_controller(...), register_exception_handler(...), register_middleware(...).
from patera import development, ignore
from patera.controller import Controller, get, path


@path("/debug")
@development              # only exists with DEBUG=True
class DebugApi(Controller):
    ...


@ignore                   # never registered
@path("/legacy")
class LegacyApi(Controller):
    ...

items.title: Application package name
items.text: The application package is called app by default. If yours has another name, set the APP_PACKAGE option and the PATERA_APP_PACKAGE environment variable for the patera command (see Running the application).

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
A Patera project is a Python package, by default called app:

my-app/
  app/
    __init__.py          # the application class
    configs.py           # configuration
    api/
      __init__.py
      greeting_api.py    # controllers are discovered automatically
    templates/
    static/
  .env
  pyproject.toml

items.title: 1. Configuration
items.text:
app/configs.py:

import os

from patera import BaseConfig


class Config(BaseConfig):
    BASE_PATH: str = os.path.dirname(__file__)  # required
    APP_NAME: str = "My app"
    VERSION: str = "1.0.0"

BASE_PATH is the directory of the application package. Every option can also be set from the environment; see Configuration.

items.title: 2. The application class
items.text:
app/__init__.py:

from patera import Patera, app

from .configs import Config


@app(__name__, configs=Config)
class App(Patera[Config]):
    pass

@app supplies the runtime metadata (the import name and the configuration class); the generic argument Patera[Config] gives your editor and type checker the configuration type.

items.title: 3. A controller
items.text:
app/api/greeting_api.py:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from patera import HttpStatus, MediaType, Request, Response
from patera.controller import Controller, consumes, get, path, post, produces

from app import App


class Greeting(BaseModel):
    name: str


@path("/api/v1/greetings")
class GreetingApi(Controller[App]):
    @get("/")
    @produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    async def hello(self, req: Request) -> Response:
        return req.res.json({"message": "Hello, World!"})

    @post("/")
    @consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    @produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON, HttpStatus.CREATED)
    async def greet(self, req: Request, greeting: Greeting) -> Response:
        return req.res.json({"message": f"Hello, {greeting.name}!"})

The controller lives in an api folder and its file name contains api, so Patera discovers it automatically.

items.title: 4. Run it
items.text:
uv run patera dev

Open http://localhost:3000/api/v1/greetings/. Send a POST with a JSON body {"name": "Ana"} to the same URL to call greet; an invalid body is answered with 422 and the validation errors.

The generated API documentation is available at http://localhost:3000/openapi/docs.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• Project layout: which folders and file names are discovered.
  • Controllers: routes, parameters, validation and hooks.
  • Services and dependency injection: structure your business logic.
  • Testing: test your endpoints with PateraTestClient.

items.title: Running the application
items.text:
The patera command finds your application class automatically: it looks for the class decorated with @app in app/__init__.py, app/app.py, app/main.py, ... Use --app module:Class or the PATERA_IMPORT environment variable to point at it explicitly, and PATERA_APP_PACKAGE if your package is not called app.

Command Description patera dev [--app app:App] [--env-file .env] Development server (Uvicorn) with auto-reload. Loads .env, .env.dev or .env.local if no file is given. Host and port from PATERA_HOST/PATERA_PORT (default localhost:3000). patera prod [--app app:App] [--env-file .env.prod] Production server (Granian, installed with the prod extra), DEBUG is forced off. Only an environment file given with --env-file is loaded. Host and port from PATERA_HOST/PATERA_PORT (default 0.0.0.0:80), event loop from PATERA_LOOP. patera cli Controller:command [args...] Runs a CLI command. patera agents [codex\|claude\|all] Generates coding-agent instructions and Patera skills without loading an application. patera test [--env-file FILE] [pytest args...] Runs pytest after loading the test environment file (.env.test when the project has one). See Testing. DevelopmentProduction 
uv run patera dev

uv add "patera[prod]"
uv run patera prod --env-file .env.prod

items.title: Environment files
items.text:
• patera dev and application CLI commands load an explicit --env-file, or search .env, .env.dev and .env.local in that order.
  • patera prod loads only an environment file named with --env-file.
  • patera test loads .env.test when present; an explicit --env-file must exist.
  • Values already present in the process environment win over values from the file.

items.title: Address
items.text:
The address is resolved in this order:

  1. PATERA_HOST / PATERA_PORT environment variables,
  2. defaults set on your configuration class (HOST, PORT),
  3. launcher defaults: localhost:3000 for dev, 0.0.0.0:80 for prod.

In production, localhost is mapped to 0.0.0.0. Configure the deployment address explicitly.

items.title: Other ASGI servers
items.text:
The application class is an ASGI application factory, so any ASGI server works:

uvicorn app:App --factory --lifespan on

Keep lifespan enabled

Startup and shutdown hooks (database connections, schedulers, caches, ...) depend on the ASGI lifespan protocol. Simply calling App() does not start resource hooks.

See Deployment for production advice.

items.title: Guide
items.text: The guide explains every feature of the core patera package. Each page can be read on its own; read them in order for a complete tour.

items.title: Fundamentals
items.text:
• Configuration: typed settings from classes and environment variables.
  • The application class: lifecycle hooks, extensions and useful members.
  • Services and dependency injection: singleton services and Inject[...].

items.title: HTTP
items.text:
• Controllers and routing: endpoints, route parameters, validation and hooks.
  • Requests: headers, bodies, forms, files and request context.
  • Responses: JSON, templates, streaming, files, cookies and response models.
  • Exception handling: handler classes and default error responses.
  • Middleware: wrap the request chain.
  • CORS: cross-origin settings, globally and per endpoint.
  • WebSockets: socket endpoints in controllers.

items.title: Content
items.text:
• Templates: Jinja2 rendering.
  • Static files and static pages: files and controller-less HTML pages.
  • OpenAPI: generated specification and Swagger UI.

items.title: Operations
items.text:
• Logging: Loguru, JSON Lines log files, custom sinks and request observers.
  • Command line interface: CLI controllers and commands.
  • Testing: PateraTestClient and patera test.
  • Coding agents: generate instructions for Codex and Claude.

items.title: Building on Patera
items.text: • Custom extensions: write reusable services and packages.

items.title: The application class
items.text:
The application is a subclass of Patera, decorated with @app:

from patera import Patera, app, on_shutdown, on_startup
from patera.injectable import Inject

from .configs import Config
from .database import Databases
from .services.greetings import GreetingService


@app(__name__, configs=Config)
class App(Patera[Config]):
    app_extensions = [Databases]   # extensions created at startup
    greetings: Inject[GreetingService]

    @on_startup
    async def start(self) -> None:
        self.logger.info("Starting")

    @on_shutdown
    async def stop(self) -> None:
        self.logger.info("Stopping")
  • @app(__name__, configs=Config) supplies runtime metadata. The import name determines the application root used for discovery, templates and static files.
  • Patera[Config] supplies typing for self.configs.
  • BASE_PATH is a directory, not a URL prefix. Use URL_PREFIX for controller URLs.

items.title: Lifecycle hooks
items.text:
Methods decorated with @on_startup and @on_shutdown run during the ASGI lifespan.

  • Startup and shutdown hooks run in alphabetical order of their method names. Use a single hook per event that calls other methods in the order you need.
  • If a startup hook raises, the server is notified that startup failed.
  • Extensions add their own hooks with app.add_on_startup_method(...) and app.add_on_shutdown_method(...); these are appended after the application's startup hooks. Do not assume a database is connected in an application startup hook.
  • Construction is distinct from the lifespan: calling App() does not run the hooks. Servers, patera dev/prod and PateraTestClient run them.

items.title: Extensions
items.text: Infrastructure services listed in app_extensions are constructed even if nothing injects them. Other services are created on first injection. See Services and dependency injection.

items.title: Background tasks
items.text:
run_in_background() from patera starts short local work that should not delay the response. Running tasks are tracked, and shutdown waits for them up to BACKGROUND_TASKS_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT seconds (default 10.0, None for no limit) before cancelling them.

Warning

Background tasks are not a durable queue. Pass plain data and acquire fresh resources inside the task: a copied context does not extend the lifetime of a request's database session. For scheduled or persistent work, use the task manager.

items.text: Member Description configs, get_conf(name, default=None) configuration url_for(endpoint, **params) URL of an endpoint ("Controller.method", "alias.method", "static") get_extension(cls), extensions registered extensions/services get_controller(cls_or_name), controllers registered controller instances register_controller(*classes) register controllers manually register_exception_handler(*classes) register exception handlers manually register_middleware(cls, order=None) register middleware manually (before the first request) add_template_path(path) additional template folder add_on_startup_method(fn), add_on_shutdown_method(fn) lifespan hooks add_request_observer(fn) observe every completed HTTP request (see Logging) json_spec the OpenAPI specification (dict) logger the Loguru logger root_path, static_files_path, app_name, version paths and metadata url_prefix the URL_PREFIX setting ("" without a prefix) default_exception_response(req, exc) override to customize the default error responses

items.title: Custom request and response classes
items.text: Set REQUEST_CLASS / RESPONSE_CLASS in the configuration to use subclasses of Request and Response throughout the application.

items.title: Command line interface
items.text: Besides running servers, the patera command runs application commands: maintenance tasks, imports, database migrations and anything else you write as a CLI controller. The built-in commands are listed in the CLI reference.

items.title: CLI controllers
items.text:
Commands are methods of CLI controllers:

# app/cli/maintenance_cli.py
from patera.cli import CLIController, cli_controller, command


@cli_controller(name="maintenance")
class MaintenanceCLI(CLIController):

    @command("greet", help="Greets a user")
    async def greet(self, name: str, times: int = 1) -> None:
        for _ in range(times):
            print(f"Hello, {name}!")

uv run patera cli maintenance:greet Ana 3
uv run patera cli --list          # list application commands and their help
  • Arguments are positional and converted according to the parameter annotations (str, int, float, bool, optional single types and other callables). Parameters with defaults are optional. Named options are not parsed.
  • A failing command prints the error and exits with status code 1.
  • CLI controllers support dependency injection like any other component; inject services for the business logic.
  • Controller aliases (name=) must be unique.

Select an application or environment file explicitly:

uv run patera cli --app app:App --env-file .env.tools maintenance:greet Ana

items.title: CLI mode
items.text:
The application is created in CLI mode: no HTTP server, no middleware, and no ASGI lifespan. Acquire and close resources explicitly:

  • database commands can use @cli_session("main") from patera.database.sql, which opens a session and a transaction for the command (see SQL databases),
  • HTTP clients such as an API interface need aclose() in finally.

HTTP request middleware and HTTP transaction decorators do not apply to commands.

items.title: Commands from extensions
items.text:
Extensions register CLI controller instances (unlike HTTP controllers, which are registered as classes):

self.app.register_cli_controller(GreetingCLI(self.app))

This is how migrations (migrate:*), the desktop extension (desktop:*) and desktop UI (ui:*) add their commands.

items.title: Coding agents
items.text:
Patera can generate instructions and a Patera skill for AI coding agents such as Codex and Claude. Run the command from the project directory, even before an application exists:

patera agents             # AGENTS.md and .agents/skills/patera/
patera agents claude      # CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills/patera/
patera agents all         # both layouts; CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md
patera agents all --dry-run

The bundled skill covers application construction, configuration, injection, controllers, requests and responses, middleware, errors, CLI controllers, WebSockets, templates, logging, testing, deployment, custom extensions and all official extension packages. Its SKILL.md routes to focused reference files. Generation works offline from the installed package and does not require the optional extensions.

items.title: Behaviour
items.text:
• Existing instruction files keep their content outside a marked Patera section.
  • Repeated runs skip identical files.
  • A conflicting skill file stops generation before any writes; use --force to replace the bundled files deliberately. Unrelated files are preserved.
  • --dry-run never writes, even with --force.
  • Malformed section markers and linked destinations require manual repair and are not bypassed by --force.
  • The command writes to the current directory, without searching for an app or loading environment files. The application options --app, --env-file and --list do not apply.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Configuration classes inherit from patera.BaseConfig, a pydantic-settings model:

import os

from patera import BaseConfig


class Config(BaseConfig):
    BASE_PATH: str = os.path.dirname(__file__)   # required
    APP_NAME: str = "My app"
    SECRET_KEY: str                              # required, e.g. from PATERA_SECRET_KEY

Settings are validated when the application is constructed, so set environment values before constructing the app.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Every option can be overridden with an environment variable prefixed with PATERA_. Nested values use __ as separator:

PATERA_DEBUG=false
PATERA_PORT=8080
PATERA_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS='["https://app.example.com"]'
PATERA_MAIN_DB__DATABASE_URI=postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@db/app

Values usually live in .env files; see Running the application for which file each command loads.

items.title: Extension and component settings
items.text:
Extension, service and middleware settings are regular fields of your config class, named after the class in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: MainDb → MAIN_DB, PublicCache → PUBLIC_CACHE. Renaming the class changes the key.

from patera import BaseConfig
from patera.caching import CachingConfig


class Config(BaseConfig):
    BASE_PATH: str = os.path.dirname(__file__)
    PUBLIC_CACHE: CachingConfig = CachingConfig(DURATION=30, MAX_SIZE=500)

A nested dictionary is validated against the component's configuration model; an absent configuration uses the model's defaults if it has no required fields. See Services and dependency injection.

items.title: Settings from the environment only
items.text:
The values can live in .env (or the environment) instead of the class. Declare a settings model without a value, and it is built from the variables that are set, with the model's defaults for the rest:

class Config(BaseConfig):
    BASE_PATH: str = os.path.dirname(__file__)
    MAIN_DB: SqlDatabaseConfig    # PATERA_MAIN_DB__DATABASE_URI must be set
    DESKTOP: DesktopConfig        # every field has a default; PATERA_DESKTOP__WIDTH=1200 changes one

A required field that no variable sets stops the application at startup with its name (MAIN_DB.DATABASE_URI: Field required). A model declared with a value in the class (MAIN_DB: SqlDatabaseConfig = SqlDatabaseConfig(...)) keeps that value as its default, and variables change single fields of it.

items.title: Reading configuration
items.text:
• app.configs.NAME: typed attribute access.
  • app.get_conf("NAME", default): supports dotted paths into nested models and dictionaries, for example app.get_conf("MAIN_DB.DATABASE_URI") or app.get_conf("DEFAULT_LOGGER.LEVEL").
  • The ConfigVar descriptor in controllers and services:
from patera.injectable import ConfigVar


@path("/greetings")
class GreetingApi(Controller["App"]):
    app_name: str = ConfigVar("APP_NAME")
    label: str = ConfigVar("GREETING_LABEL", "Greetings")   # with default

ConfigVar reads settings through the application lookup path; it does not declare a required Pydantic field.

items.title: Built-in options
items.text:
The most important built-in options are BASE_PATH, APP_NAME, VERSION, DEBUG, HOST, PORT, URL_PREFIX, MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH and the CORS_*, OPEN_API*, TEMPLATES_* and STATIC_* groups. The complete table with defaults is in the configuration reference.

Use the model, not guesses

patera.configuration_base.BaseConfig is the source of truth for exact field names and defaults. See the API reference.

items.title: Controllers and routing
items.text:
A controller is a class that groups endpoints under a base path:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from patera import HttpStatus, MediaType, Request, Response
from patera.controller import (
    Controller, after_request, before_request, consumes, delete, get, path, post, produces,
)

from app import App


class UserIn(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: str


class UserOut(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str


@path("/api/v1/users", tags=["Users"], alias="users")
class UserApi(Controller[App]):

    @get("/")
    async def list_users(self, req: Request) -> Response[list[UserOut]]:
        return req.res.json([{"id": 1, "name": "Ana"}])

    @get("/<int:user_id>")
    async def get_user(self, req: Request, user_id: int) -> Response[UserOut]:
        return req.res.json({"id": user_id, "name": "Ana", "password_hash": "..."})

    @post("/")
    @consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
    @produces(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON, HttpStatus.CREATED)
    async def create_user(self, req: Request, user: UserIn) -> Response[UserOut]:
        return req.res.json({"id": 2, "name": user.name})

    @delete("/<int:user_id>")
    async def delete_user(self, req: Request, user_id: int) -> Response:
        return req.res.no_content()

    @before_request
    async def before(self, req: Request) -> None:
        ...  # runs before every endpoint of this controller

    @after_request
    async def after(self, res: Response) -> None:
        res.set_header("x-controller", "users")

Controller instances are shared across concurrent requests: keep request data in local variables or the request context, not on self.

items.title: The controller decorator
items.text:
@path(url, open_api_spec=True, tags=None, alias=None) sets the base path of the controller.

  • alias is an alternative name for url_for: url_for("users.get_user", user_id=1). The class name always works too: url_for("UserApi.get_user", user_id=1).
  • Several controllers may share a base path.
  • tags group the endpoints in OpenAPI; open_api_spec=False hides the controller from the specification.
  • URL_PREFIX from the configuration is prepended to every controller route.

items.title: Endpoints
items.text:
@get, @post, @put, @patch, @delete(url, open_api_spec=True, tags=None) declare endpoints.

  • The first argument after self is always the Request; route parameters are passed as keyword arguments.
  • Handlers may be async or plain functions; plain functions run in a thread pool.
  • Duplicate route definitions are errors (DuplicateRouteError).

items.title: Route parameters
items.text:
Route parameters use Werkzeug converters, not {name} syntax:

Pattern Matches <name> a string without slashes <int:id> an integer <float:x> a float <uuid:key> a UUID <path:rest> a string including slashes

Query parameters do not become handler arguments. Read them from req.query_parameters and validate them with req.validate(Model, data) (see Requests).

items.title: Request bodies and validation
items.text:
@consumes(MediaType) requires the request to have this content type (otherwise 415). Parameters annotated with a Pydantic model are validated from the JSON body, url-encoded form or multipart form (including UploadedFile fields).

  • For forms, a single value of a field the model declares as a list (checkboxes, multi-selects) arrives as a one-item list.
  • Invalid data raises RequestValidationError: 422 with the validation errors, without the submitted values, unless you handle it yourself.

items.title: Responses and response models
items.text:
@produces(MediaType, status_code=HttpStatus.OK) sets the default media type and status code. An explicitly set content type or status wins (also .status(HttpStatus.OK)). Both are documented in OpenAPI.

Annotating the return type as -> Response[Model] validates and serializes the body through Model, which filters out undeclared fields (password_hash above):

  • generic annotations such as list[Model] or dict[str, Model] filter every item,
  • dictionaries, model instances and objects with matching attributes (ORM rows) are accepted,
  • only 2xx bodies are shaped this way; error bodies keep their own fields,
  • the annotation also documents the response in OpenAPI.

items.title: Controller hooks
items.text: Decorator Runs @before_request before every endpoint of the controller; receives the request @after_request after every endpoint; receives the response @after_init once, after the controller is created and its dependencies are injected

items.title: Other endpoint decorators
items.text: Decorator Purpose @open_api_docs(Descriptor(status, description, media_type, body)) document additional (error) responses @cors(...) / @no_cors per-endpoint CORS settings @max_content_length(limit) override MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH for one endpoint (None for no limit) @development the endpoint (or controller) only exists in debug mode @ignore never registered @socket(url) a WebSocket endpoint

items.title: Routing behaviour
items.text:
• With STRICT_SLASHES=False (default), /users and /users/ reach the same endpoint.
  • Unknown paths return 404 (JSON). A known path with the wrong method returns 405 with an Allow header.
  • HEAD requests are answered by the matching GET endpoint, without a body.
  • OPTIONS requests to routes without an explicit handler return 204 with an Allow header (CORS preflight requests are answered by the CORS middleware).

items.title: Building URLs
items.text:
Use url_for instead of assembling prefixed URLs by hand. It is available on the application and in templates:

self.app.url_for("UserApi.get_user", user_id=1)   # class name
self.app.url_for("users.get_user", user_id=1)     # alias
self.app.url_for("static", filename="site.css")   # static files

Endpoint names default to Class.method. Keep controller and CLI alias spaces distinct.

items.title: CORS
items.text:
CORS is enabled by default and configured with the CORS_* options:

Option Default Description CORS_ENABLED True Global CORS handling. CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS ["*"] Allowed origins. CORS_ALLOW_METHODS ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"] Allowed methods. CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS ["Authorization", "Content-Type"] Allowed request headers. CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS [] Response headers exposed to the browser. CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS False Allow cookies and Authorization on cross-origin requests (the request origin is echoed instead of *). CORS_MAX_AGE None Preflight cache time in seconds. 
PATERA_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS='["https://app.example.com"]'
PATERA_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=true

items.title: Behaviour
items.text:
• The middleware answers preflight requests (OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method) and adds CORS headers to all responses of allowed origins, including error responses.
  • Requests from origins that are not allowed are processed normally but without CORS headers, so the browser blocks cross-origin reads while same-origin requests keep working. Preflights from such origins get 403.
  • Every response of a route with CORS enabled carries Vary: Origin, so shared caches keep the variants apart.

Credentials

Turn on CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS only together with an explicit CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS list, and declare specific methods and headers. CORS is not authentication or CSRF protection.

items.title: Per endpoint
items.text:
from patera.controller import cors, no_cors

@get("/partner-data")
@cors(allow_origins=["https://partner.example.com"], allow_credentials=False, max_age=600)
async def partner_data(self, req: Request) -> Response: ...

@get("/internal")
@no_cors
async def internal(self, req: Request) -> Response: ...

items.title: Custom extensions
items.text:
Extensions are services that plug into the application: they can register controllers, middleware, exception handlers, CLI commands, template folders and lifecycle hooks. The official extension packages are built this way.

from pydantic import BaseModel

from patera import BaseExtension, Patera


class AuditConfig(BaseModel):
    ENABLED: bool = True


class AuditService(BaseExtension[Patera, AuditConfig]):
    def init(self) -> None:
        if self.configs.ENABLED:
            self.app.add_on_startup_method(self.start)
            self.app.add_on_shutdown_method(self.stop)

    async def start(self) -> None:
        self.app.logger.info("Audit started")

    async def stop(self) -> None:
        self.app.logger.info("Audit stopped")

Declare AUDIT_SERVICE: AuditConfig = AuditConfig() on the application's config for nested environment settings, and register the class in app_extensions or inject it. The two generic parameters are the application type, then the configuration type.

items.title: Construction and init()
items.text:
Construction resolves injections, registers the instance, then calls the synchronous init(). Prefer that hook over overriding __init__. In init(), use the application's public methods:

Register Method controller classes app.register_controller(...) middleware classes (before the chain is built) app.register_middleware(cls, order) exception handler classes app.register_exception_handler(...) CLI controller instances app.register_cli_controller(instance) template folders app.add_template_path(path), app.add_template_prefix(prefix, path) lifecycle callbacks app.add_on_startup_method(fn), app.add_on_shutdown_method(fn) request observers app.add_request_observer(fn)

Registration is provisional until init() succeeds. A failed construction rolls back framework registries, routes, template paths and lifecycle hooks, including nested dependency registrations, and injection rejects instances still initializing. This cannot undo arbitrary external side effects: acquire resources in startup, or clean them up yourself if initialization fails.

items.title: Guidelines
items.text:
• Acquire resources in startup and release them in shutdown. CLI users must manage resources explicitly, because commands do not run the lifespan.
  • Keep request state in the request context, never on the instance.
  • Keep instances independent, so several test applications can coexist.
  • Validate settings rather than silently ignoring invalid values.
  • Extension class names must not collide within one application.
  • Do not import the concrete application into a reusable extension; type against Patera.

items.title: Publishing an extension
items.text: Publish reusable extensions as separate distributions. Official packages install under the patera namespace, whose path is extended by the core; a third-party package can use its own import namespace. Include templates and static resources in the distribution and test an installed artifact, not only editable sources. Follow the naming conventions in the public API reference.

items.title: Services and dependency injection
items.text:
Application services are subclasses of BaseExtension (alias: Service). Each service is a singleton per application. Declare dependencies with Inject[...] on the application class, controllers, services, middleware, exception handlers or CLI controllers: they are created on first use and shared.

from pydantic import BaseModel

from patera import Request, Response, Service
from patera.controller import Controller, get, path
from patera.injectable import ConfigVar, Inject


class GreetingSettings(BaseModel):
    PREFIX: str = "Hello"


class Formatter(Service):
    def format(self, prefix: str, name: str) -> str:
        return f"{prefix}, {name}!"


class GreetingService(Service["App", GreetingSettings]):
    formatter: Inject[Formatter]

    def init(self) -> None:          # called after construction
        self.greeted = 0

    def greet(self, name: str) -> str:
        self.greeted += 1
        return self.formatter.format(self.configs.PREFIX, name)


@path("/greetings")
class GreetingApi(Controller["App"]):
    greetings: Inject[GreetingService]
    app_name: str = ConfigVar("APP_NAME")

    @get("/<name>")
    async def greet(self, req: Request, name: str) -> Response:
        return req.res.text(self.greetings.greet(name))

items.title: How resolution works
items.text:
• Dependencies are class annotations, resolved before init() on services and before @after_init hooks on controllers.
  • There is one instance per application, with no request or transient scope. Do not store the current user, request or database session on a service.
  • Registry keys derive from class names; distinct classes with the same name collide.
  • Injectable classes must accept the application as their only constructor argument. Wrap libraries that need other constructor arguments in a service.
  • Circular dependencies are reported with CircularDependencyError instead of providing partially initialized objects. Break them by separating responsibilities.
  • Injection also works with from __future__ import annotations, as long as the injected class is importable at runtime (not only under TYPE_CHECKING).

items.title: Interfaces and implementations
items.text:
There is no automatic resolution by superclass. For an interface with a concrete implementation, use Autowire:

from typing import Annotated

from patera.injectable import Autowire, Inject


class NotesApi(Controller["App"]):
    storage: Annotated[Storage, Autowire(FileStorage)]

items.title: Service configuration
items.text:
self.configs of a service returns the configuration field named after the class in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (GreetingService → GREETING_SERVICE). The second type argument of Service[...] / BaseExtension[...] declares the configuration model, which means:

  • a configuration model instance in the config class is used as is,
  • a plain dict (for example from PATERA_GREETING_SERVICE__PREFIX=Hi) is validated with the model,
  • a missing configuration falls back to the model's defaults, or raises a clear error if the model has required fields.
class Config(BaseConfig):
    BASE_PATH: str = os.path.dirname(__file__)
    GREETING_SERVICE: GreetingSettings = GreetingSettings(PREFIX="Welcome")

items.title: Creating services at startup
items.text:
Services that must exist from startup (for example to register hooks or middleware) are listed in App.app_extensions; others are created when they are first injected. List order alone does not establish all dependency ordering, since injection can construct a service earlier.

Retrieve any service with app.get_extension(GreetingService).

To write reusable services with their own controllers, middleware and lifecycle hooks, see Custom extensions.

items.title: Exception handling
items.text:
Exception handlers are classes with methods mapped to exception types:

from patera import HttpStatus, Request, Response
from patera.exceptions import (
    BaseHttpException,
    ExceptionHandler,
    RequestValidationError,
    exception_handler,
    handles,
)


class EntityNotFound(BaseHttpException):
    def __init__(self, message: str):
        super().__init__(message, HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)


@exception_handler
class ApiExceptionHandler(ExceptionHandler):

    @handles(RequestValidationError)
    async def validation_error(self, req: Request, exc: RequestValidationError) -> Response:
        return req.res.json({"message": "Invalid data", "details": exc.errors}).status(422)

    @handles(BaseHttpException)          # also handles subclasses, e.g. EntityNotFound
    async def http_error(self, req: Request, exc: BaseHttpException) -> Response:
        return req.res.json({"message": exc.message, "data": exc.data}).status(exc.status_code)

Put the class in an exceptions folder (file name containing handler) or register it with app.register_exception_handler(...).

  • @handles accepts several exception classes and can be stacked.
  • A handler registered for a base class also handles its subclasses; lookup follows the exception's MRO and the most specific handler wins.
  • Exceptions raised in middleware are handled by the exception handlers too.

A handler can return any response, for example RFC 9457 problem details:

@handles(MissingNote)
async def missing(self, req: Request, exc: MissingNote) -> Response:
    return req.res.problem("Note not found", str(exc), 404)

items.title: Default responses
items.text:
Without a matching handler:

Exception Response BaseHttpException and subclasses (abort(), authentication errors, ...) JSON {"status", "message", "data"} with the exception's status code RequestValidationError (from @consumes or req.validate(), a BaseHttpException) 422 with {"status": "error", "message": "Validation failed", "data": [...]} anything else, including a pydantic.ValidationError from your own code or data DEBUG=True: the exception propagates (traceback in the server log). DEBUG=False: 500 {"status": "error", "message": "Internal server error"} and the error is logged

Other built-in statuses: a malformed body is 400, a media type mismatch 415, an oversized body 413.

Override default_exception_response(req, exc) on the application class to change this fallback.

items.title: Quick aborts
items.text:
from patera import HttpStatus, abort, html_abort

abort("User not found", HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, data={"id": user_id})   # JSON error response
html_abort("errors/404.html", HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, {"id": user_id})  # renders the template

items.title: Special cases
items.text:
• HtmlAborterException and StaticPageNotFound have special dispatch: register their exact classes to replace their handling. A generic BaseHttpException handler does not capture them.
  • Routing failures (404, 405) occur outside ordinary controller and middleware handling.
  • The framework resets unfinished responses before replacing them with an error. Once sending has started (for example a stream), failures propagate without sending a second response; disconnects cannot be answered either.
  • Response[Model] conversion does not apply to 4xx/5xx bodies. Build and validate an error schema explicitly if you need one.

items.title: Logging
items.text:
Patera logs with Loguru. Use self.app.logger in controllers and services (or app.logger).

self.app.logger.info("Note created")
self.app.logger.bind(note_id=note.id).warning("Note title truncated")

items.title: The default sink
items.text:
The default console sink is configured with DEFAULT_LOGGER, a DefaultLoggerConfig model. Fields you leave out keep their defaults, and unknown fields are rejected:

from patera.logging import DefaultLoggerConfig


class Config(BaseConfig):
    ...
    DEFAULT_LOGGER: DefaultLoggerConfig = DefaultLoggerConfig(
        SINK="STDERR",             # STDERR, STDOUT, NULL or a file path
        LEVEL="INFO",
        ENQUEUE=True,
        COLORIZE=True,
    )

Fields can also be set from the environment, for example PATERA_DEFAULT_LOGGER__LEVEL=INFO.

items.title: Log files
items.text:
Every record at LOG_FILES.LEVEL or above is also written to a JSON Lines file, one JSON object per line with time, level, message, logger_name, name, file, line, function, process, thread, and, when present, exception (the formatted traceback) and extra (values bound with logger.bind(...)). The admin dashboard reads its log view from these files.

from patera.logging import LogFilesConfig


class Config(BaseConfig):
    ...
    LOG_FILES: LogFilesConfig = LogFilesConfig(
        PATH="logs/patera.jsonl",  # relative to the application package; must end with .jsonl
        LEVEL="INFO",
        ROTATION="10 MB",          # size, time of day ("00:00") or interval ("1 day"); None = never
        FILE_COUNT=5,              # files kept, including the active one
    )
Field Default Description ENABLED True Write log files. PATH logs/patera.jsonl Active file. Rotated files are renamed with their rotation time, e.g. patera.2026-10-09_13-25-00_123456.jsonl. LEVEL DEBUG Minimum level written. ROTATION 10 MB When the active file is rotated. FILE_COUNT 5 Number of files kept; older rotated files are deleted. ENQUEUE True Write from a background queue. READ_LIMIT 10000 Maximum number of newest records returned by app.log_files.read().

app.log_files.read(limit) (or await app.log_files.read_async(limit)) returns the newest records, oldest first.

Several workers

Rotation is not coordinated between processes. With several server workers appending to one file, set ROTATION=None and rotate with an external tool, or run a single worker.

items.title: Custom sinks
items.text:
Additional sinks are classes in a logging / loggers folder (file name containing logger, log_sink or logging):

# app/loggers/file_logger.py
from patera.logging import LoggerBase, logger


@logger("File logger")
class FileLogger(LoggerBase):
    def get_filter(self):
        return lambda record: record["level"].no >= 30   # WARNING and above

Its settings are read from the config field named after the class:

class Config(BaseConfig):
    ...
    FILE_LOGGER: dict[str, Any] = {
        "SINK": "logs/app.log",     # relative to the application package
        "LEVEL": "WARNING",
        "ROTATION": "5 MB",
        "RETENTION": "10 days",
        "COMPRESSION": "zip",
    }

Override the sink getters as needed; configs_model selects the settings model. Loguru is process-global, so applications in the same process share its sinks.

Note

Built-in request logging includes the query string. Redact at the logging boundary or avoid sensitive URL parameters.

items.title: Request observers
items.text:
For HTTP metrics, register an observer, typically from a service listed in app_extensions:

from patera import RequestRecord, Service


class RequestMetrics(Service):
    def init(self):
        self.app.add_request_observer(self.observe)

    def observe(self, record: RequestRecord):
        if record.duration > 1:
            self.app.logger.warning(f"Slow request: {record.method} {record.path}")
  • Observers see static requests and routing failures that middleware misses, and run after the response is sent.
  • Records include the method, path, matched route (or None), sent status, start time and duration in seconds.
  • Keep callbacks quick. Failures are logged and skipped, and an observer cannot change the response.

items.title: Middleware
items.text:
Middleware wraps the request handling chain:

# app/middleware/timing_mw.py
import time

from patera import Request, Response
from patera.middleware import MiddlewareBase, middleware


@middleware(order=10)
class TimingMiddleware(MiddlewareBase):
    async def middleware(self, req: Request) -> Response:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        res = await self.next(req)          # or return a response directly (short-circuit)
        res.set_header("x-process-time-ms", str(int((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)))
        return res

items.title: Registration
items.text:
Middleware is discovered in middleware folders (file names containing middleware or mw) or registered explicitly before the first request:

app.register_middleware(TimingMiddleware, order=10)

An extension registers its middleware classes in init().

items.title: Order
items.text:
Lower order numbers run first (outermost): they enter first and exit last. Built-in middleware uses negative orders:

Middleware Order CORS -101 SQL session manager (database) -100 Authentication -99

Give application middleware distinct positive orders. If an order is taken, the next free number is used and a warning is logged.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: Middleware can declare a configuration model just like services: MiddlewareBase[App, MyConfig], available as self.configs and read from the config field named after the class (TimingMiddleware → TIMING_MIDDLEWARE). Middleware supports dependency injection with Inject[...].

items.title: What middleware does not see
items.text:
• Routing precedes the middleware chain.
  • Static files bypass middleware, so middleware cannot protect static assets.
  • WebSockets have a separate path; HTTP middleware is not applied to them.
  • Middleware is a singleton: keep per-request values in locals or the request context.

To observe every completed HTTP response, including static files and routing failures, use a request observer.

Exceptions raised in middleware are handled by the exception handlers.

items.title: OpenAPI
items.text:
With OPEN_API=True (default), the specification is served at /openapi/specs.json and a Swagger UI at /openapi/docs.

The specification is generated from your controllers:

Source Becomes routes and path parameters paths @consumes + Pydantic parameters request bodies @produces and Response[Model] annotations responses @open_api_docs(Descriptor(...)) additional (error) responses @path(tags=...), endpoint tags=... tags docstrings descriptions 
from patera.controller import Descriptor, open_api_docs


@get("/<int:user_id>")
@open_api_docs(Descriptor(404, "User not found", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON, ErrorBody))
async def get_user(self, req: Request, user_id: int) -> Response[UserOut]:
    """Returns one user."""
    ...

Exclude a controller or endpoint with open_api_spec=False.

The document's server is relative (URL_PREFIX, or /), so "Try it out" calls the origin that served the page, behind a proxy too.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Option Default Description OPEN_API True Serve the specification and Swagger UI. OPEN_API_URL "/openapi" Base URL of the documentation. OPEN_API_DESCRIPTION "Simple API" Description in the specification. APP_NAME / VERSION Title and version of the specification.

The specification is also available in code as app.json_spec.

Tip

Use @consumes, @produces and @open_api_docs from patera.controller for incoming HTTP endpoints, not the identically named decorators of the API interface. Verify the generated schema after changing annotations.

items.title: Requests
items.text:
Every endpoint receives a Request as its first argument after self.

Member Description method, path, query_string, headers (lower-case keys) request line and headers query_parameters dict; repeated keys become lists query_list(name) all values of a query parameter as a list route_parameters parsed route parameters await body(), await json() raw body / parsed JSON (None if empty; malformed JSON is 400) await form(), await files(), await form_and_files() url-encoded and multipart data await form_list(name) all values of a form field as a list validate(Model, data) validates client data the handler reads itself await get_data(location) "json", "form", "files", "form_and_files" or "query" user, roles, set_user(), set_roles() authenticated user (see Authentication) context request-scoped storage app, res / response the application and the response being built

items.title: Bodies
items.text:
Parsing is lazy. Await req.body(), req.json(), req.form(), req.files() or req.form_and_files() as needed; do not consume the ASGI receive channel yourself.

@post("/notes")
async def create(self, req: Request) -> Response:
    data = await req.json()
    return req.res.json({"title": data["title"]}).status(201)
  • An empty body gives None; malformed JSON is answered with 400.
  • A broken multipart body is answered with 400.
  • A body larger than MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH (default 10 MB, override per endpoint with @max_content_length) is answered with 413.
  • A client that disconnects mid-body raises ClientDisconnected: the handler stops and no response is sent.

For JSON and forms that map to a model, prefer @consumes with a Pydantic parameter; see Controllers.

items.title: Uploaded files
items.text:
Files are UploadedFile objects (importable from patera):

Member Description filename, content_type, size metadata sent by the client read(), seek() read like a file save(path) write to disk stream the underlying stream 
@post("/avatars")
async def upload(self, req: Request) -> Response:
    files = await req.files()
    avatar = files["avatar"]
    avatar.save(os.path.join(self.upload_dir, f"{uuid4()}.png"))
    return req.res.no_content()

Warning

Pick safe storage names rather than trusting the upload's filename, and never store private uploads under the public static directory.

items.title: Validation
items.text:
req.validate(Model, data) validates client data the handler reads itself, such as query parameters or route values. Invalid data raises RequestValidationError, answered with 422:

class Paging(BaseModel):
    page: int = 1
    per_page: int = 20


@get("/")
async def index(self, req: Request) -> Response:
    paging = req.validate(Paging, req.query_parameters)
    ...

A plain pydantic.ValidationError raised elsewhere in your code is an application failure, not a client error. Use req.validate for user input.

items.title: Request context
items.text:
req.context is request-scoped storage:

req.context.set("trace_id", trace_id)
trace_id = req.context.get("trace_id")

The current request is also available anywhere during request handling through patera.ctx.current_request. It exposes set/get, the request and the application; has_request_context() checks whether a request is active.

from patera.ctx import current_request

current_request.set("trace_source", "http")

Use the context (or local variables) for per-request data; never store it on controllers, services or middleware, which are shared singletons.

items.title: Responses
items.text:
Each request carries the response being built as req.res. Its methods return the response, so calls can be chained:

return req.res.json({"ok": True}).status(HttpStatus.CREATED).set_header("x-id", "7")

Response is tied to the application and the request: always start from req.res rather than constructing a response with only a body.

items.title: Body methods
items.text: Method Description json(data) JSON body: dicts, lists, Pydantic models and values inside them such as dates, UUIDs and decimals, encoded as Pydantic encodes them. A str or bytes raises TypeError (use text(), or bytes(data, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON.value) for encoded JSON) text(), html_body(), xml(), csv(), yaml(), ndjson(rows), bytes(data, media_type) other bodies await html(template, context), await html_from_string(source, context) rendered templates problem(title, detail, status, type_="about:blank", instance=None, extra=None) RFC 9457 problem details stream(iterable, media_type), stream_text(iterable) streaming responses (sync or async iterables) redirect(location, status=303), no_content() redirects and 204

items.title: Status and headers
items.text:
Method Description status(code) status code (int or HttpStatus) set_header(), set_headers() headers set_cookie(name, value, max_age, path, domain, secure, http_only, same_site) set a cookie delete_cookie(), add_raw_cookie() delete or add a raw cookie

Choose secure, http_only and same_site deliberately for session cookies.

items.title: Response models
items.text:
Annotate an endpoint with -> Response[Model] to validate and filter successful bodies through a Pydantic model. See Controllers.

The renderer validates and converts 2xx data before middleware completes. Error bodies are not validated against the success model.

items.title: Streaming
items.text:
@get("/export")
async def export(self, req: Request) -> Response:
    async def rows():
        try:
            async for row in self.reports.rows():
                yield row
        finally:
            await self.reports.close()

    return req.res.ndjson(rows())

After the first chunk is sent, the status and headers can no longer change: an error is logged and the connection is closed. Release resources in finally.

items.title: Files
items.text:
file_response(res, path, req.headers, download_name=...) from patera.utilities streams a file from disk, with range requests, ETag and 304 support. download_name makes it a download under any file name.

from patera.utilities import file_response


@get("/reports/<int:report_id>")
async def download(self, req: Request, report_id: int) -> Response:
    path = self.reports.path_for(report_id)        # authorize before serving
    return file_response(req.res, path, req.headers, download_name=f"report-{report_id}.pdf")

Serve private files through an authorized controller like this, never from the static folder.

items.title: Aborting
items.text: abort() and html_abort() raise HTTP exceptions that become error responses; see Exception handling.

items.title: Static files
items.text:
Files in STATIC_DIR are served at STATIC_URL (/static/<path:filename>) with:

  • Content-Type detection,
  • HTTP range requests (206 Partial Content, useful for media),
  • path traversal protection.
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='site.css') }}">
Option Default Description STATIC_DIR / STATIC_URL "static" / "/static" Static files folder and URL prefix. STATIC_CONTROLLER_NAME "static" url_for alias for static files.

Static files are public

Static files bypass middleware, including authentication. Use the static folder only for public assets and serve private downloads through an authorized controller (see Responses). Static URLs are not prefixed by URL_PREFIX.

In production, consider serving static files with a reverse proxy instead.

items.title: Static pages
items.text:
With USE_STATIC_PAGES=True, HTML files in STATIC_PAGES_DIR are rendered as Jinja templates and served under STATIC_PAGES_URL without writing a controller:

File URL pages/about.html /about or /about.html pages/docs/intro.html /docs/intro

Pages can extend and include each other by name. Build links with url_for("static_pages", page="about").

Option Default Description USE_STATIC_PAGES False Serve HTML pages from STATIC_PAGES_DIR. STATIC_PAGES_DIR / STATIC_PAGES_URL "static_pages" / "/" Static pages folder and URL prefix. STATIC_PAGES_CONTROLLER_NAME "static_pages" url_for alias for pages.

A missing page raises StaticPageNotFound; register a handler for that exact class to customize the response (see Exception handling).

items.title: Templates
items.text:
Templates are rendered with Jinja2 (async, auto-escaping for HTML/XML) from TEMPLATES_DIR (default templates, relative to the application package):

@get("/")
async def index(self, req: Request) -> Response:
    return await req.res.html("index.html", {"title": "Home"})

<h1>{{ title }}</h1>
<a href="{{ url_for('UserApi.list_users') }}">Users</a>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='site.css') }}">

await req.res.html_from_string(source, context) renders a template from a string.

items.title: Template context
items.text:
Besides your context, templates receive:

Name Value app the application request the current request url_for URL building, as on the application attribute getattr len len

items.title: Settings
items.text: Option Default Description TEMPLATES_DIR "templates" Template folder, relative to BASE_PATH. TEMPLATES_STRICT True Undefined template variables raise errors. AUTO_RELOAD True Reload changed templates.

items.title: Template folders
items.text:
The application's own template folder always takes precedence over folders added by extensions or static pages. Extensions add folders with app.add_template_path(path) or namespaced folders with app.add_template_prefix(prefix, path).

Warning

Keep auto-escaping enabled for untrusted values and use url_for rather than hard-coded application paths, so URL_PREFIX is respected.

items.title: HTML error pages
items.text: html_abort("errors/404.html", HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, {"id": user_id}) renders a template as an error response; see Exception handling.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
patera.testing.PateraTestClient runs the application (including startup and shutdown hooks) and sends requests through HTTPX. It needs the testing extra, which also installs pytest and pytest-asyncio:

uv add --dev "patera[testing]"

items.title: A first test
items.text:
# tests/conftest.py
import pytest

from patera.testing import PateraTestClient
from app import App


@pytest.fixture
async def client():
    async with PateraTestClient(App()) as c:
        yield c

# tests/test_users.py
async def test_list_users(client):
    res = await client.get("/api/v1/users/")
    assert res.status_code == 200

The client offers get, post, put, patch, delete, head, options and request, which all accept the usual HTTPX keyword arguments such as json=, headers= and files=.

The async context manager runs the lifespan. A bare HTTPX ASGI transport does not run startup and shutdown hooks.

items.title: Configure pytest
items.text:
# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
asyncio_mode = "auto"
asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope = "function"

items.title: Run the tests
items.text:
uv run patera test              # loads .env.test if present
uv run patera test -k login -q  # pytest options in any order
uv run patera test -- -x        # everything after -- goes to pytest unchanged
uv run pytest                   # plain pytest

patera test --env-file FILE loads another environment file, which must exist.

items.title: Good practice
items.text:
• Set test configuration and environment variables before constructing the app.
  • Use a fresh app and isolated databases, files and caches for independent tests.
  • Test production error behaviour with DEBUG disabled when asserting generic 500 bodies.
  • Cover input failures, authorization, transaction commit/rollback, response models and lifecycle cleanup.
  • Mock external SMTP, HTTP and AI transports instead of sending real requests.
  • Use a socket harness for WebSockets and isolated argv/output/filesystem for CLI commands.

items.title: WebSockets
items.text:
WebSocket endpoints are controller methods decorated with @socket:

from patera import Request
from patera.controller import Controller, path, socket


@path("/ws")
class ChatSocket(Controller[App]):
    @socket("/chat/<room>")
    async def chat(self, req: Request, room: str) -> None:
        if (await req.receive())["type"] != "websocket.connect":
            return
        await req.accept()
        while True:
            message = await req.receive()
            if message["type"] == "websocket.disconnect":
                break
            if message["type"] == "websocket.receive" and "text" in message:
                await req.send({"type": "websocket.send", "text": f"[{room}] {message['text']}"})

Socket handlers receive and send the raw ASGI messages through req.receive() / req.send() and accept the connection with req.accept(). Their routes include URL_PREFIX. The development server needs the websockets package, included in the dev extra.

items.title: Differences from HTTP endpoints
items.text:
• Sockets send ASGI messages directly, not rendered Response objects.
  • HTTP middleware and controller @before_request / @after_request hooks do not run.
  • A socket handler (or its controller, including inherited metadata) marked with @login_required, @role_required or @transactional is refused at startup. Check the user inside the handler and keep sockets in a controller of their own.
  • Unexpected exceptions close the connection with code 1011.

items.title: Security and resources
items.text:
• Validate credentials and the allowed origin explicitly before accepting a private socket.
  • Use short-lived sessions for database operations, never a transaction for the whole connection. Database sessions a socket handler opens through Model.query() or a repository are closed when it returns, and uncommitted work rolls back.
  • Release resources in finally, handle disconnects and bound your queues.

items.title: Testing
items.text: PateraTestClient sends HTTP requests only. Test sockets through an ASGI WebSocket harness or a real socket client.

items.title: Changelog
items.text: All notable changes to Patera and its extension packages. Until version 1.0, a minor release may contain breaking changes; they are listed first in each release.

items.title: Stabilization fixes
items.text:
• Core: failed extension initialization rolls back framework registrations, routes, template paths and lifecycle callbacks. Injection cannot reuse an instance still initializing. Ordinary subclass overrides now remove inherited injection declarations, following the Python MRO.
  • Caching: response caching defaults to GET/HEAD. Explicitly opt into other methods with methods=("POST",); these keys include a request-body digest. Default handler keys now use module and qualified names. Update manual cache invalidation patterns using the former short names. key also accepts a synchronous or asynchronous function of the request.
  • Task manager: persisted-job dispatch uses an optional stable JOB_NAMESPACE. Conflicting active managers are rejected instead of silently replacing another application's manager; registrations end at shutdown.
  • API interface: standalone/CLI calls close temporary HTTP clients within their event loop. Lifespan calls continue to share a client. Explicit client access requires closing in the owning loop before switching loops.
  • Desktop: shutdown waits for reloader children, with bounded forced cleanup using psutil. Settings tests no longer spoof the whole interpreter platform.
  • JoltUI: structured error responses from decorators and lifecycle hooks preserve their status and media type. Successful component responses still require HTML. Brand spelling and package metadata are consistent.
  • Public API: exported MigrateConfig (old private alias retained), added patera[desktop-ui], and documented existing names and the [all] server bundle in PUBLIC_API.md. Desktop UI now includes author, project and maturity metadata.
  • Release verification: explicit candidate/final versions are supported by the bump helper. Added isolated wheel installation checks, a browser-bootstrap syntax check, and a Python 3.13/3.14 CI matrix for Windows, Linux and macOS.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• patera-database: SqlDatabaseConfig.SQLITE_FOREIGN_KEYS (default False) runs PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON on every new SQLite connection, so FOREIGN KEY constraints such as ON DELETE CASCADE are enforced; SQLite leaves them off by default. Set it in the settings model or from the environment, for example PATERA_MAIN_DB__SQLITE_FOREIGN_KEYS=true. Other databases ignore it. Applications no longer need to override SqlDatabase.connect() for this.
  • patera-database: SqlDatabaseConfig.SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT (seconds, default None) runs PRAGMA busy_timeout on every new SQLite connection: how long a connection waits for another connection's lock before failing with "database is locked". None keeps the driver's default of 5 seconds, or a ?timeout= in DATABASE_URI; a value takes precedence over both. Other databases ignore it, for example PATERA_MAIN_DB__SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT=10.
  • patera-admin: FileInput and DateInput form elements in patera.admin.custom_elements, for Meta.custom_form_fields. FileInput renders <input type="file"> (with accept and a browser-side max_size); the model's admin hooks receive the chosen file as an UploadedFile, and when no file is chosen the field is not sent, so an update keeps the current value. DateInput renders a date or, with include_time=True, a date-and-time picker; its value is converted to the column's type like a generated input, and utc=True shows a stored UTC timestamp in the viewer's local time and submits it in UTC. Custom elements opt in to that conversion with converts_value = True.

  • patera-admin: LatexInput form element: a textarea, or a text input with multiline=False, for text with LaTeX math, with a preview underneath that updates while the user types. Math goes between $...$ or $$...$$, and \$ is a literal dollar sign. The preview is rendered as MathML by Temml 0.14.0 (MIT), which Admin serves from its own static assets (js/vendors/temml/) and loads only on pages with this input. The inner control is an ordinary form field, so it is submitted and validated with the form.

  • Core: request observers. app.add_request_observer(callback) calls callback(record) after every HTTP request, including router answers (404, 405), static resources and failed requests, with a patera.RequestRecord: method, path, the matched URL rule (/api/exams/<exam_id>, or None when no route matched), the status sent (500 for a failure before the response started), the start time and the duration. An observer that raises is logged and skipped; applications without observers take the previous code path. Router.path_of(endpoint) returns an endpoint's URL rule.

  • patera-admin: request statistics on the dashboard, above the logs: uptime and start time, requests and average requests/s, 2xx/4xx/5xx counts with their share, average and approximate 95th-percentile response time, a stacked requests-per-second chart by status class, a response time chart, the busiest endpoints and the most frequent 4xx/5xx statuses with their routes, for the last 15 minutes, hour, 6 hours or 24 hours, refreshed every 10 seconds. Admin collects them in memory through a request observer (24 hours, 10-second buckets), so each worker shows its own requests since it started; the dashboard's own polling is not counted. AdminConfig.REQUEST_STATISTICS=False turns the collection and the section off. The data is served as JSON at <ADMIN_BASE_URL>/<lang>/dashboard/stats?period=1h.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• patera-admin: the log table's page links no longer run off the right edge when there are many pages. Like the records table, they show the first and last page and two pages on each side of the current one, with ellipses between; on small screens only the neighbouring pages and arrow buttons are shown, and the links wrap if space runs out. Both tables share one template macro (_admin/layout/pagination.html) and patera.admin.pagination.page_items().
  • Core: a Response[Model] body made of ORM objects is converted through its declared type as soon as the route handler returns, while the request's database sessions are still open. Before, it was converted when the response was sent, after patera-database had rolled back (requests without @transactional) or committed with EXPIRE_ON_COMMIT=True and closed the session, so reading the expired objects failed with DetachedInstanceError (500). A body that does not fit its type now fails inside the middleware chain, so a @transactional request is rolled back instead of committed; the answer is still 500. Streamed bodies are not converted early, and relationships must be loaded eagerly. patera.serializers.materialize() and ResponseRenderer.materialize_body() perform the conversion.
  • patera-admin: record dialogs no longer overflow the window: the form inside each dialog is now the flex column, so the header and footer stay visible and the body scrolls.
  • patera-admin: a custom form element gets its own id in the create and update dialogs (create-field-<name>, update-field-<name>); both used create-field-<name>, and the update dialog's label pointed at the create form. Elements without content, such as <input>, are rendered without a closing tag.
  • patera-admin: a model's admin_delete() hook can refuse a deletion by raising AdminFormError: Admin answers 422 with the first error's message, which the records table shows (it was a 500).
  • patera-admin: an unknown database or model in a records-table URL shows the Admin error page with 404 (rendering the page failed because the template context was missing).
  • patera-admin: the sign-in and "unauthorized" pages load Bootstrap and its icons from the copies shipped with the package instead of jsDelivr, so Admin works without internet access.

items.title: patera 0.121.0 and extensions 0.11.0 (2026-10-12)
items.text: Every package in this release requires patera>=0.121. Upgrade the core and the extensions together.

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
• patera-auth: signed cookie values carry a signing timestamp (value|timestamp|signature). Values signed by earlier versions are rejected, which signs users out once.
  • patera-caching: Redis and SQLite keys default to the prefix patera:<app name>:<cache name>: instead of patera:cache: (Redis) or no prefix (SQLite), so existing cache entries are not found. Set KEY_PREFIX to keep the old keys. BaseCacheBackend.from_configs() takes a namespace argument, and configure_from_app() is gone; use backend_class or from_configs().
  • patera-migrate: .pyway.conf no longer contains connection details. The connection, including the password, is read from DATABASE_URI each time a command runs. The file stays in the migration directory and in .gitignore; regenerate it with migrate:init (delete the old one first) or remove the connection lines, because a database_* value left in the file overrides the URI.
  • patera-admin: Slovenian uses the ISO code sl instead of si (URLs, DEFAULT_LANGUAGE).
  • patera-apiinterface: a 4xx or 5xx response raises ApiInterfaceResponseError instead of being returned as data. Request forwarding is opt-in with @forward_request; method arguments fill <name> placeholders and become query parameters or the body.
  • patera-database: @query methods annotated -> None return None; -> int on a statement without result rows returns the number of affected rows.
  • Core: a settings model declared in the config class without a value (MAIN_DB: SqlDatabaseConfig) is built from the environment (and .env), with the model's defaults for the fields no variable sets; with no variable at all, from the defaults alone. A required field that nothing sets is reported by name (MAIN_DB.DATABASE_URI), instead of the whole model being "required".
  • Core: Granian is no longer installed with the core package. patera prod needs the new prod extra: uv add "patera[prod]" (or pip install "patera[prod]"); without it, the command says so. The core's own dependencies are now pure Python apart from pydantic-core.
  • Core: blank query and form values (?q=) are kept as "" instead of being dropped.
  • Core: the OpenAPI document's server is relative (URL_PREFIX, or /) instead of PROTOCOL://HOST:PORT, so Swagger's "Try it out" calls the origin that served the page.
  • Core: patera test loads .env.test only when it exists (an explicit --env-file must exist), runs pytest without arguments by default so pytest's own configuration (testpaths) applies, and no longer has the unused --app option.
  • Core: Response.set_cookie() raises ValueError for names or values a browser would change (spaces, ;, ,, quotes, backslashes, control characters) and for SameSite=None without secure=True.
  • Core: a request header sent several times is combined into one comma-separated value (Cookie with ;); use Request.header_list() for the separate values.
  • Core: loggers read their settings only under the UPPER_SNAKE_CASE name of their class.
  • Core: removed patera.utilities.get_range_file(), get_file() and Response.send_file(); use file_response(), which streams the file and takes a download_name.
  • Core: CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS defaults to False: by default no website may make cross-origin requests with the user's cookies. Set it to True together with an explicit CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS list for a frontend on another origin.
  • patera-admin: a signed-in user without the needed Admin permission gets 403 instead of 401 (with "status": "error"), and an unknown database name gets 404.
  • Core: the @app_path decorator is replaced by the URL_PREFIX setting (PATERA_URL_PREFIX), so the prefix can differ per environment: @app_path("/demo") becomes URL_PREFIX: str = "/demo" in the configuration class. The value must start with /; a trailing / is removed. Patera.url_prefix returns it, and register_controller(with_base_path=...) is now with_url_prefix=....
  • Core: invalid @consumes data raises RequestValidationError (a BaseHttpException): 422 with {"status", "message", "data": [errors]}, without the submitted values. Handle RequestValidationError instead of pydantic.ValidationError; its errors attribute is the list. A ValidationError raised anywhere else (handler code, data from a database or another service) is a server error (500) instead of a 422 that echoed the values. Validate query parameters and other client data with the new req.validate(Model, data).
  • Core: res.json() raises TypeError for str and bytes; use text(), or bytes(data, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON.value) for already encoded JSON.
  • Core: UploadedFile.read(size) reads like a file, from the current position onwards (it always returned the first bytes, so chunked readers never finished).
  • Core: two controller classes with the same name raise ValueError at startup (the second was silently skipped). A WebSocket handler, or its controller, marked with @login_required, @role_required or @transactional raises ValueError at startup: middleware does not run for sockets, so these had no effect.
  • Core: removed the unused patera.request.extract_boundary().
  • patera-admin: every action needs ADMIN_CAN_ENTER and its own permission (VIEW, CREATE, EDIT, DELETE); ADMIN_CAN_ENTER alone allowed every action. Give administrators all five.
  • patera-admin: record forms of models without a validation schema are converted to the column types, and only the fields the form shows are written: a field excluded from the form can no longer be set by adding it to the request. An unticked checkbox sets False.
  • patera-taskmanager: @schedule_job jobs without an id get <class>.<method> instead of a random id, and every declared job replaces its stored copy at startup.
  • patera-caching: responses are cached as the bytes that are sent, and the Redis and SQLite backends store JSON instead of pickle. Existing entries are treated as misses.
  • Core: dropped the unused dependencies h11, httpcore, idna, mako and markupsafe; websockets moved to the dev extra (used by the uvicorn development server). httpx and asgi-lifespan, used only by the test client, moved to the testing extra: install patera[testing] to use patera.testing.PateraTestClient.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Core: MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH (default 10 MB) and the @max_content_length decorator; larger bodies get 413.
  • Core: BACKGROUND_TASKS_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT (default 10 s): on shutdown the application waits for run_in_background() tasks before closing resources, then cancels and logs the rest.
  • Core: STARTUP_BANNER setting; the startup line is always logged.
  • Core: patera dev and patera prod resolve the address from PATERA_HOST/PATERA_PORT, then the config class defaults, then localhost:3000 (dev) or 0.0.0.0:80 (prod), and the application reports the address actually used.
  • Core: patera cli without a command name lists every command.
  • Core: Request.cookies, Request.header_list(), Request.query_list(), Request.form_list().
  • Core: static files (and Admin static files) send ETag, Last-Modified and Cache-Control, answer conditional requests with 304, honour If-Range, and are always sent zero-copy.
  • Core: NDJSON streaming with ndjson_line(); SerializerRegistry.register(first=), replace() and unregister().
  • Core: DuplicateRouteError and CircularDependencyError with clear messages.
  • Core: is_async_callable() and wait_for_background_tasks() utilities; py.typed marker.
  • Core: Request.validate(), RequestValidationError, ClientDisconnected and Request.response_started.
  • patera-auth: role_required(..., require_all=True) requires every listed role.
  • patera-auth: decode_signed_cookie(..., max_age=...) rejects old values.
  • patera-auth: new password hashes are bcrypt-sha256$ + bcrypt over a SHA-256 digest, so passwords of any length count in full. Plain bcrypt hashes from earlier versions still verify; password_hash_needs_update() tells you when to store a new hash after a successful login.
  • patera-admin: severity filter for log records, notifications (admin.notify(), the header bell, failed e-mail sends recorded automatically), the application and Admin versions in the footer, and extension discovery on every request.
  • patera-apiinterface: ApiInterfaceResponseError; -> httpx.Response returns the raw response unchecked; NDJSON responses are parsed line by line; one shared HTTPX client per event loop, closed at shutdown (create_client(), aclose()).
  • patera-caching: per-user cache entries by default (per_user, user_cache_key()), backend_class, Caching.cache_name.
  • patera-database: background_session() and SqlDatabase.session_scope() for work outside a request; SqlDatabase.work_session() for a service's own work (the request's session in a @transactional request, its own transaction elsewhere), request_session() and in_transactional_request().
  • patera-email: USE_SSL (implicit TLS), HTML messages with a generated plain-text alternative, and Date and Message-ID headers on every message.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• Core: uploaded files are no longer altered: the body is parsed as received (part headers were rewritten anywhere in the body, including inside file content). Field and file names are decoded as UTF-8.
  • Core: JSON bodies may contain models, lists of models, dates, UUIDs, decimals and enums (they failed with 500), and Response[list[Model]] and other generic annotations filter every item like Response[Model] does; ORM objects are accepted too. NDJSON rows are encoded the same way. The declared type shapes only 2xx bodies, so error bodies such as the 415 from @consumes keep their own fields.
  • Core: file_response(download_name=...) writes a correct Content-Disposition for names in any language (content_disposition()).
  • Core: an explicit middleware order of 0 is kept.
  • Core: an error after a streamed or file response has started is logged and the connection is closed, instead of a second response being attempted.
  • Core: a client that disconnects before its body has arrived raises ClientDisconnected; the truncated body was handled as if it were complete. No response is sent.
  • Core: a malformed multipart body (missing or wrong boundary) answers 400 instead of 500.
  • Core: a form field the @consumes model declares as a list accepts a single value.
  • Core: a controller property that needs a request (current_request.user) no longer fails at registration.
  • Core: raw non-UTF-8 bytes in a query string no longer fail the request before a response.
  • Core: CLI arguments annotated Optional[int] or int | None are converted.
  • Core: @produces(..., status_code) no longer overrides an explicit .status(200) (Response.status_set).
  • Core: every response of a route with CORS enabled carries Vary: Origin, also without an Origin header, for a refused origin and for routing errors, so shared caches keep the variants apart.
  • Core: logging works again when the application's lifespan runs a second time (the shutdown removed the sinks for good).
  • patera-admin: record forms of models without a validation schema failed for boolean columns (always) and number and date columns (PostgreSQL); records with an integer key could not be viewed, edited or deleted on PostgreSQL. Values and keys are converted to the column types.
